objects.svg: The six photographs are arranged in two rows: frog, eagle and elephant above tiger, penguin and gorilla. They introduce objects whose relationships can depend on appearance, biological category or other properties. The layout is a display grid, not a fitted similarity map.
stimulus_028.png: A photograph depicts a tiger. The animal is the referent; the photograph is one depiction; a pixel array is a numerical encoding of that photograph. This distinction does not imply that a neural response has the same meaning as either encoding.
appearance.svg: Left: the original tiger photograph. Middle: the same photograph with its pixel intensities multiplied by one half, making it darker. Right: a gorilla photograph. The first change preserves object identity while changing image values; the second changes the depicted object.
pixel_vector.svg: The tiger photograph is represented as 224 by 224 single-channel values, then reduced to 28 by 28 pixels. These 784 values are listed in row order to form a vector. The static illustration wraps the vector into seven display bands; the interactive version shows selected entries as code.
neural_response.svg: A broad coronal MRI from Bao et al. (2020), Figure 4c, shows functionally localized IT patches at the middle level in monkey M3. Beside it, a tightly cropped axial detail from Extended Data Figure 8a marks three example recording sites in the Stubby2 patch and retains its 5 mm scale. These separate views are anatomical context, not registered slices or locations of all 482 neurons. A light frame encloses the original monochrome cat stimulus. The plot preserves all 482 unit positions and the original response values. Its vertical axis runs from 0 to 100; the largest value is about 80.75. There are 479 available values. Small vertical marks below the axis identify unavailable measurements at positions 429, 430 and 457; they are not zeros. These NaNs already occur in the original shared matrix; the paper does not explain their cause. Bao retained every well-isolated neuron encountered at functionally targeted sites, without a separate visual-selectivity ANOVA screen. The experiment used 1,224 rendered views, 250 ms presentation and 4–8 repeats; activity was analyzed 60–220 ms after onset. A1 describes the export as firing rates, but its exact scaling and baseline processing are undocumented, so this figure does not label the values as calibrated Hz.
network_stages.svg: A conceptual sequence connects image, early layers, later layers and class scores. Each layer computes a new pattern from the preceding one. This is an introduction to sequential processing, not a complete diagram of AlexNet or ResNet: residual connections and architecture-specific operations are omitted.
matched_network.svg: The input is exactly the Bao stimulus shown with the IT recording. A bar chart shows its first 32 stored late ResNet18 activation entries. The supplied vector has 4,096 sampled entries from flattened spatial activations, not 4,096 channels. The measurements come from an ImageNet-trained model. Matching the image allows a comparison; it does not establish a correspondence between individual neurons and network entries.
bold_response.svg: A BOLD5000 photograph of a dog appears beside two bar charts for participant CSI1: the early visual region on the left and lateral occipital complex on the right. Each chart shows the first 16 voxels in stored order, from 210 and 152 voxels respectively. Values can fall above or below the processed baseline. These Release 1 ROI measurements average TR3/TR4 after stimulus onset; they are blood-oxygenation-related responses, not firing rates or Release 2 beta estimates. This is a separate dataset from the matched Bao IT/network example.
features_point.svg: Six images are plotted using mean intensity and RMS contrast. The tiger is highlighted at approximately (72.7, 40.6), with dashed guides to its two components. The next slide keeps exactly these axes and measurements and replaces its point marker with the head of a vector from the origin.
features_vector.svg: The identical coordinate frame and image positions as the preceding slide. A blue vector runs from the origin to the tiger at approximately (72.7, 40.6). The selected point marker is removed so the arrowhead is visible. Its label x is bold; scalar component axis labels are italic. These are static slide builds, not an automatic animation.
more_coordinates.svg: Three columns describe the same BOLD5000 response using the first two voxels, the first three, and all 210 early visual voxels. The initial entries stay the same as the list grows. In the last column, a vertical ellipsis omits middle entries and the final displayed value is component 210. Adding dimensions means retaining more components; it does not require inventing extra directions on a two-dimensional page.
response_matrix.svg: Rows are the six recurring animal photographs; columns are the first 12 stored network activation entries. Each colored cell gives an activation for one image and one entry. A row is an image's response vector. The displayed matrix is a subset of the six by 4,096 matrix; color intensity is not a similarity score.
peterson2018_fig3a_animals_mds.png: Three published nonmetric multidimensional-scaling maps show the same animal images, using human judgments, raw network representations, and a learned transformation of network features. Each map places images so their separations approximate the corresponding comparisons. The maps illustrate how object relationships can change when the representation changes. Their display axes are not particular neurons or features. Orientation and overall placement are arbitrary; visual resemblance alone does not quantify agreement. These are the authors' fitted maps, not a new result computed for this lecture.
scaling.svg: Illustrative vector x=(3,1) runs from the origin to (3,1). Multiplication by two produces 2x=(6,2), along the same direction at twice the length. Both components are multiplied by the scalar. The smaller arrow lies on the longer vector's direction by construction. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
addition.svg: Illustrative x=(3,1) and y=(1,3) start at the origin. Translating y so its tail is at x's endpoint gives the sum endpoint (4,4), without changing y's length or direction. Dashed guides complete the parallelogram. The mean, (x+y)/2=(2,2), is halfway from the origin to the sum. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
size_words.svg: Photographs of a frog, tiger, gorilla and elephant illustrate the animal words. The semantic-projection model receives word representations, not these photographs. The question is whether a direction through word-vector space can recover judgments about animal size.
difference.svg: The displacement from x=(3,1) to y=(1,3) is y−x=(−2,2): two units left and two units up. The vector is drawn from x's endpoint to y's endpoint, unlike a position vector drawn from the origin. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
dot_product.svg: Vectors x=(3,1) and w=(1,1) begin at the origin. The marked angle phi is the angle between them. Their dot product is 3×1+1×1=4, also equal to the product of their lengths and cosine of phi. Here w has length square root of two; the following projection example normalizes this direction. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
projection.svg: Vector x=(3,1) is projected onto the unit vector w=(1,1)/√2. A dashed direction line extends w. The perpendicular guide from x's endpoint meets the direction at p=(2,2); the right-angle marker records this perpendicularity. The scalar projection is wᵀx=2√2, while the projected vector is p=(wᵀx)w. The residual x−p=(1,−1) is orthogonal to w. The unit vector itself has length one. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
semantic-projection.png: The published schematic places animal-word vectors in an embedding space and projects them onto a direction associated with small versus large. Perpendicular drops convert the vectors into scalar positions along that direction. Those scores can be compared with human size judgments. The illustration is schematic, not a measured two-dimensional embedding or an accuracy plot. The paper combines anchor pairs to define directions; a readable direction alone does not establish that the model uses it causally.
structured_pixels.svg: The reduced tiger image appears beside an array of independently sampled random grayscale values. Both occupy the same 784-dimensional pixel space. The comparison illustrates that naturally structured images occupy a restricted part of the possible pixel configurations; the random array is a teaching illustration, not a measured neural response.
euclidean.svg: Object A is at (3,1) and object B at (1,3). Their differences along the two axes have magnitudes two and two. Dashed perpendicular legs form a right triangle; the connecting segment has length √(2²+2²)=√8. A and B name objects, not matrices. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
distance_ranking.svg: The illustrative response patterns are A=(1,1), B=(4,4) and C=(1,−1). A and B have the same direction but different lengths; C is perpendicular to A. Euclidean distance ranks C closer to A: d(A,C)=2 versus d(A,B)=√18. Cosine dissimilarity ranks B closer: dcos(A,B)=0 versus dcos(A,C)=1.
relu.svg: The rectified linear unit is flat at output zero for negative inputs, passes through the origin, and has output equal to input for positive inputs. Negative preactivation therefore produces a zero activation. A unit that is inactive for every sampled image creates an all-zero column in a response matrix.
dead_column.svg: Two image rows are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0). The third unit is zero for both images. Without that column, each row's mean is one half and the correlation is −1. With it, each row's mean is one third and the correlation is −0.5. Appending the shared zero changes row centering while preserving Euclidean distance and cosine similarity in this example.
animal_rdm.svg: A square matrix compares every pair of the six animal images using Euclidean distance between all 4,096 stored late ResNet18 entries. Row and column labels have the same order. The diagonal is zero and the matrix is symmetric. Off-diagonal cells summarize relationships between whole response vectors, not single-unit responses. The numeric alternative below contains every plotted distance.
triangle_bound.svg: A path travels from A to B by a segment of length one, then from B to C by a second segment of length one. Endpoint separation is at most two; the displayed straight path attains the maximum. Bending the path cannot place the endpoints farther apart. This motivates the triangle inequality.
cosine_triangle.svg: Three unit vectors have directions zero, 45 and 90 degrees. Cosine dissimilarity between the extreme directions is one. Each adjacent dissimilarity is 1−1/√2, approximately 0.293; their sum is approximately 0.586, less than one. Thus cosine dissimilarity violates the triangle inequality, despite being symmetric and nonnegative for these vectors.
11_same_score.svg: The schematic contrasts internal point arrangements of models with equal task accuracy. A single performance score does not uniquely determine internal response geometry. The point layouts are illustrative, not fitted empirical embeddings, and do not by themselves establish which model better explains brain responses.
basis.svg: The same vector (3,2) in the standard basis is expressed in a rotated orthonormal basis with e₁=(1,1)/√2 and e₂=(−1,1)/√2. Its rotated coordinates are 5/√2 and −1/√2, approximately 3.536 and −0.707, respectively. Recombining those coordinates with the rotated basis vectors reconstructs (3,2). The vector and its length stay fixed while its coordinates depend on the basis.
codes.svg: Three illustrative six-stimulus by eight-unit matrices contrast coding patterns. Localist: each stimulus activates a distinct single unit. Dense distributed: each stimulus uses all units with varying strengths. Sparse distributed: each stimulus activates two units. These examples describe how a population pattern can distribute information; they are not recorded data or definitions of every possible coding scheme.
network_maps.svg: The model input is the same Bao cat image as the IT recording, converted to RGB and center-cropped to 224 by 224. The figure shows channels 1 and 2 at the early, middle and late ResNet18 stages. Their spatial grids are 56 by 56, 14 by 14 and 7 by 7, respectively; the full stages contain 64, 256 and 512 channels. Light color denotes zero; color intensity increases to the maximum for that image and stage, shared across its channels. Scales can differ between stages. These are actual CPU-computed responses using A1 weights and preprocessing, verified against the stored readouts. The live explorer also includes layer2, six images, all channels and a numeric table of the selected map. A unit is a channel at a spatial position; a channel is not a single scalar. Class predictions in the explorer are model outputs, not ground-truth object labels.
spike_to_rate.svg: Illustrative schematic, not an observed trial. A tungsten electrode beside a neuron detects extracellular spikes. Seven example spikes fall in a 160 millisecond window, from 60 to 220 milliseconds after image onset. Dividing seven spikes by 0.16 seconds gives 43.75 spikes per second, or 43.75 Hz. Bao et al. used this post-onset window to count responses; the local matrix export scaling remains a separate provenance question.
pixel_bars.svg: Left: the same tiger photograph used in the pixel explorer. Middle: its 28 by 28 grayscale version. Right: all 784 grayscale values as bars, read left to right across each row and then down to the next row. Each bar denotes one pixel, and height is intensity on a 0–255 scale. Pixel index is spatial ordering, not time. The bar plot contains exactly the values shown in the grayscale image. Its panel layout matches the later cat neural-response figure, where the entries refer to neurons instead of pixels; no neural recordings are asserted for this tiger.
network_vector.svg: The actual Bao cat input is passed through ImageNet-trained ResNet18. In the late readout, channel 376 has a 7 by 7 spatial map. Reading rows in order gives 49 scalar activations; the first four are 0.00, 1.80, 2.41, 2.36. Concatenating the 512 channel vectors in order gives 25,088 values. Flattening preserves the values and does not average spatial positions. A1 uses a fixed sample of 4,096 entries from the full flattened layer. The static channel is selected by largest spatial mean; the interactive explorer supports every channel and all four stages.
bold_surface_vectors.svg: The surface illustration locates two BOLD5000 functional regions: red early visual cortex and green lateral occipital complex (LOC). The colors label localizer-defined regions, not response magnitude or activation for the dog. These maps are cropped from Gao et al. 2025 Figure 6b, which does not name the participant. Beside them are the exact presented ImageNet dog photograph and all 210 early visual and 152 LOC response values for participant CSI1, left hemisphere, trial index 8. Each bar is one voxel in the stored order. These Release 1 processed BOLD values average TR3 and TR4 and are not firing rates. Each region provides an ordered response vector.
electrode_to_rate.svg: A tiger photograph is presented to a simplified macaque visual pathway, shown in the original lateral diagram from DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust (2012), Figure 3A. The retina projects to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), followed here by V1, V2, V4 and inferotemporal cortex (IT). The animation omits feedback and parallel routes, and its timing is illustrative. The next panel shows synthetic extracellular voltage and seven spike times assigned to one illustrative neuron between 60 and 220 milliseconds. Dividing seven events by 0.160 seconds gives 43.75 spikes per second, or Hz. The tiger and trace do not constitute a recorded Bao trial. Interactive panels reveal in three stages.
tigers_monkey.svg: Three unchanged photographs from the assignment animal image set, in fixed left-to-right order: A, a tiger standing on rocky ground (row28, stim-0354); B, a tiger facing the camera in water (row41, stim-0609); C, a monkey (row64, stim-0942). The two tiger photographs differ in pose, visible body parts and background while sharing the tiger category. Tiger–monkey comparisons cross categories. The figure introduces these comparisons without displaying or claiming measured similarity ratings or neural activity. A and B label photographs, not identified individual animals.
magritte-1929-lacma.webp: René Magritte’s 1929 painting The Treachery of Images, from LACMA. A brown smoking pipe appears against a beige ground above a cursive French inscription, “Ceci n’est pas une pipe” (“This is not a pipe”). The juxtaposition distinguishes an object from an image depicting it. The full source image and its original colors are preserved. Photograph © Museum Associates/LACMA; artwork credit © C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.
rgb_channels.svg: Color tiger photograph and its red, green and blue channel images. The 224 by 224 image contains 150,528 channel values. At row 112, column 112 the RGB values are [172, 129, 105], or approximately [0.675, 0.506, 0.412] after division by 255. Three bars encode those selected channel values. The interactive version allows any pixel to be selected by pointer, arrow keys or row and column controls.
tungsten-tips-en2023-fig5.jpg: Scanning electron micrographs of two tungsten microelectrode tips from Oikawa et al. (2023), Figure 5, with a 20 micrometer scale bar. These are representative physical tips, not the specific electrodes from Bao et al. The original dark microscopy background is retained. The accompanying list distinguishes tetrodes, Utah arrays, Neuropixels probes and calcium imaging.
hubel-wiesel-simple-poster.png: Still from the historical Hubel–Wiesel simple-cell film. A projected diagonal light bar crosses the screen while an experimenter marks response locations. In the film, clicks make the recorded neuron’s electrical events audible; activity changes with the bar’s position and orientation. The demonstration is from cat visual cortex, not the macaque IT dataset. A local captioned player and text description are available in the linked interactive version.
yamins-dicarlo-2016-framed.svg: Figure 1b–c: ventral-stream areas and a candidate hierarchical convolutional model. A macaque brain inset locates V1, V2, V4 and posterior, central and anterior IT. The upper pathway also includes retinal ganglion cells (RGC) and the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). Arrows connect successive populations; recurrent and feedback connections are visible. Beneath this pathway, stacked sheets represent multiple feature maps at successive CNN layers. Small red boxes identify local receptive fields; a lower-right inset identifies filtering, thresholding, pooling and normalization. Green dashed arrows indicate proposed mappings between model stages and biological populations. These are modeling hypotheses to test using neural responses, not assertions that a CNN layer is anatomically identical to a cortical area. The illustrated architecture is schematic, not AlexNet or ResNet-18. Source colors are preserved inside a thin neutral frame. The 100-ms presentation is part of this schematic, not Bao’s experiment.
imagenet-ensemble-history.svg: Selected ImageNet/ILSVRC top-5 test accuracies, plotted by benchmark year: five AlexNet-family models 83.6% (2012); Clarifai ensemble 88.3% (2013); VGG seven-model submission 92.7% and GoogLeNet seven-model submission 93.3% (2014); mixed-depth six-model ResNet ensemble 96.4% (2015). Top-5 means the reference category is among the five highest-ranked predictions. The curve connects selected historical results; different training and evaluation procedures mean it does not isolate the effect of network depth. These are ensemble scores, not the accuracy of an individual VGG-16 or ResNet-152.
trials_averaging.svg: An explicitly illustrative numerical example for one stimulus image i. The same three neurons respond over three repetitions. Repetition 1 is (2,5,1), repetition 2 is (4,3,2), and repetition 3 is (3,4,3), in spikes per second over a fixed window. Componentwise averaging gives the image mean vector x with superscript (i), equal to (3,4,2). Features keep their neuron order. These are invented trial-level rates, not observed Bao recordings or individual spike times.
transpose_column_row.svg: The mean response for image i is displayed as a 3-by-1 column vector with entries 3, 4, 2. Transposition turns it into a 1-by-3 row containing 3, 4, 2 in the same order. Bold x denotes the vector; superscript (i) identifies the image and upright T denotes transpose. The operation preserves the values. This illustrative row can then be stored as row i of a response matrix.
similarity_fallback.svg: Two newly computed nonmetric multidimensional-scaling maps of the same 120 A1/Peterson animal images: human pairwise ratings and raw ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 late activations. Each point is one stimulus image. Human dissimilarity is 10 minus the mean 0–10 rating; network dissimilarity is one minus correlation between activation vectors. The maps are independently centered and scaled for display, without alignment or a transformation fitted to human judgments. Axes are arbitrary display coordinates. These are classroom recomputations, not the published Peterson Figure 3a coordinates. The embedded explorer highlights the same stimulus in both maps and provides a larger photograph; the static figure highlights the tiger from the opening.
training_loop.svg: Supervised image-classification training, shown schematically. A training image passes through a network with adjustable weights and internal representations to produce predicted class probabilities. Comparing the prediction with the image’s true category label produces a classification loss. A learning algorithm uses this loss to update the weights. Repeating this process over labeled training images seeks a lower average loss and changes internal responses to images. After training, weights are fixed when extracting representations for analysis. The probability bars are illustrative: monkey is shown as more probable than the correct label tiger. They are not measured network predictions, and no training results are depicted.
pixel_scaling.svg: The same tiger image from the earlier pixel explorer is shown as a 28 by 28 single-channel array, then after multiplying every intensity by 0.5. The second image is darker. Beside the images, the first four entries of the original 784-entry vector and its scaled version demonstrate that every entry is halved and the order is unchanged. The images share the same black-to-white display scale, from 0 to 255; underlying scaled values retain fractions. This is a static example of the interactive multiplier.
image_blend.svg: The 28 by 28 tiger and gorilla images from the earlier pixel explorer flank their pixelwise arithmetic mean. For every location, the middle intensity is half the tiger value plus half the gorilla value. All images share the same zero-to-255 grayscale display scale. The mixture overlays image structure; it is not a morph between animal shapes. The live version varies the weight from zero (tiger) through one half (the mean) to one (gorilla).
mixup_targets.svg: A training example for mixup: the input is a 50–50 pixelwise mixture of the tiger and gorilla images. Its target assigns weight 0.5 to the tiger class, 0.5 to the gorilla class and zero to other classes. These are constructed supervision targets, not predictions from a neural network and not human similarity judgments. The same mixing coefficient is used for the image and its target.
difference-0.svg: Two position vectors share the origin. Vector x ends at (3,1), and vector y ends at (1,3). There is no connecting displacement arrow in this view. The next slide preserves the axes, labels and both vectors exactly and adds the arrow from x to y.
difference-1.svg: With both position vectors unchanged, an arrow now runs from x=(3,1) to y=(1,3). Its components are y minus x=(-2,2): two units left and two units up. The displacement arrow starts at x, unlike a position vector that starts at the origin.
projection-0.svg: Vector x=(3,1) and the true unit vector w=(1,1)/square root of two start at the origin. A dashed continuation marks the line through w. No perpendicular drop or projected vector is present yet.
projection-1.svg: The x and unit w vectors remain in exactly the same positions. A dashed perpendicular now runs from x=(3,1) to the direction line at (2,2); a small right-angle marker marks the meeting point. The projected vector is not yet drawn.
projection-2.svg: The previous perpendicular construction is unchanged. The projected vector p now runs from the origin to (2,2). Its signed length along unit w is w transpose x=2 square root of two, while p=(w transpose x)w. The residual x minus p=(1,-1) is perpendicular to w. The short magenta unit w vector retains length one.
animal_distances.svg: The three tiger photographs from the opening slide (A and B near mirror images of one another, B and C in the same walking pose) are represented by 784 pixel intensities and, separately, 4,096 stored late ResNet-18 responses. Each triangle preserves all three Euclidean distances exactly. The planes use separate display scales and have no feature axes. In pixels, B–C (same pose, same grass) is the closest pair; in network responses, A–B (the mirror pair) is the closest pair. This is a three-image illustration, not evidence about populations of images, and no human ratings were used. The live version smoothly switches between the two endpoint maps; intermediate positions are display interpolation, not intermediate network layers or training checkpoints.
image_blend_live.png: The 28 by 28 tiger and gorilla images from the earlier pixel explorer flank their pixelwise arithmetic mean. For every location, the middle intensity is half the tiger value plus half the gorilla value. All images share the same zero-to-255 grayscale display scale. The mixture overlays image structure; it is not a morph between animal shapes. The live version varies the weight from zero (tiger) through one half (the mean) to one (gorilla). This static view is captured directly from the live explorer at equal mixture, with identical image positions, controls and selected-pixel readout. The first input vector x is blue, the second input y is magenta, and the combined result is green, matching the subtraction and projection figures.
dot_product-1.svg: Vectors x=(3,1) and w=(1,1) begin at the origin. The marked angle phi is the angle between them. Their dot product is 3×1+1×1=4, also equal to the product of their lengths and cosine of phi. Here w has length square root of two; the following projection example normalizes this direction. These constructions share a fixed coordinate frame. Only the mathematical construction changes; addition and projection retain optional step controls.
shared_zeros.svg: Two actual ResNet-18 late activation profiles use the same 4,096 stored spatial features: the familiar tiger in blue and gorilla in magenta, beside their photographs. Both plots have identical horizontal and vertical scales and preserve every activation value. Green marks below each zero baseline identify the same 879 entries that are exactly zero for both images; marker height is not a negative activation. Removing those shared positions from both vectors leaves 3,217 entries. Correlation dissimilarity changes from 0.8970717146 to 1.0109306350 because each vector is recentered on a different mean. Euclidean distance remains 125.6646924 and cosine dissimilarity remains 0.6352952988. These are unmodified continuous-valued activation vectors, not binary image codes. The shared-zero criterion applies only to these two images; none of these features is zero across all 120 images.
triangle_constraint.svg: An illustrative geometric constraint, not measured animal data. Three image representations use the established labels bold x with superscripts (1), (2), and (3). Left: two segments each of length one bend through coordinates (0,0), (0.8,0.6), and (1.6,0), giving endpoint distance 1.6. Right: straightening the two segments places the three endpoints at 0,1,2 along a line; their maximum separation is two. Thus proposed RDM entries D12=1, D23=1, and D13=3 cannot all equal Euclidean distances in any dimension.
cosine_indexed.svg: Three illustrative unit image-response vectors retain the image-index notation: x^(1)=(1,0), x^(2)=(1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)), x^(3)=(0,1). Their directions are zero, 45 and 90 degrees. Cosine dissimilarity between the outer vectors is one, while the sum for the two adjacent pairs is 2-sqrt(2), about 0.586, violating the triangle inequality. Scalar coordinate axes and bold vector labels are distinct.
directional_similarity.svg: Left: a geographic locator map highlights China in blue and North Korea in magenta, with neighboring countries muted. A leader line identifies the much smaller North Korean outline. This map supplies geographic context, not a psychological distance measurement. Right: two qualitative comparison diagrams summarize the direction reported by Tversky in 1977. North Korea pointing to China is labeled higher judged similarity; China pointing to North Korea is labeled lower judged similarity. Equal-length arrows indicate comparison direction and do not encode numerical ratings, geographic distance, or an effect size. The historical example shows that reversing subject and referent can change a similarity judgment, whereas Euclidean distance is symmetric.
same_accuracy.svg: Ten real wolf and husky photographs form two rows of five. Each card gives its true label and illustrative predictions from classifiers A and B, with text and check/cross symbols for correctness. These are stipulated predictions, not trained-network outputs. Both classify seven of ten images correctly, but their three errors are disjoint: A errs on images 1, 2 and 4, all wolves in snow; B errs on image 5, a wolf in grass, and images 6 and 7, huskies with snow. B is a constructed background rule: snow predicts wolf; no snow predicts husky. A’s internal strategy is deliberately unspecified; these output labels do not establish that A uses animal evidence. The question asks which image cue explains B’s errors. Comparing representations and controlled changes to the inputs can investigate the evidence used beyond aggregate accuracy. Photo credits are linked on the slide.
rgb_live.png: All three introductory pixel views share identical panel boundaries, heading baselines, source-image position, and row/column controls. The same 224 by 224 color tiger photograph remains visible on the left; no image switching or gain control appears. The middle panel shows red, green and blue channel previews and labels 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 values. The right panel gives the selected pixel’s three encoded channel values, their rescaling by 255, a color swatch and component bars. These are original decoded color values, not reduced grayscale values.
gray_live.png: All three introductory pixel views share identical panel boundaries, heading baselines, source-image position, and row/column controls. The same 224 by 224 color tiger photograph remains visible on the left; no image switching or gain control appears. The middle panel now shows a compact 28 by 28 intensity array, with its 784-value dimension label in the same fixed position. The right panel lists the first four entries, 18, 27, 26 and 18, followed by an ellipsis, using bold x for the whole vector. It also gives the selected scalar entry and its Python index. The 8 by 8 source region is highlighted because one reduced entry summarizes that area after grayscale conversion and BOX resampling. Reshaping the resulting array changes no values.
bars_live.png: All three introductory pixel views share identical panel boundaries, heading baselines, source-image position, and row/column controls. The same 224 by 224 color tiger photograph remains visible on the left; no image switching or gain control appears. The middle panel is identical to the grayscale view. Only the right panel changes: all 784 grayscale values are plotted in row order, with a magenta highlight at the selected entry. The vertical scale is 0–255 and the horizontal axis is pixel entry, not time. These are pixel intensities, not neural responses. All values are the same as in the preceding vector view.
tiger_relu.svg: The tiger photograph used throughout the lecture is shown with its actual cached late ResNet-18 responses. All 4,096 stored spatial activation entries are plotted in their stored order. Blue stems encode the unmodified nonnegative response values. Green marks below the zero baseline identify exact zeros; the below-baseline position is only a marker row, not a negative response. There are 1,843 exact zeros, or 45.0 percent; the maximum is 13.57. The small ReLU graph shows output a_j equal to zero for nonpositive input z_j, and equal to the input for positive values. It is the response rule, not recovered preactivation data for this image. A zero for one image does not imply inactivity for every image.
